question.value: What is the pre-eruption state of T CrB and what are the properties (density, temperature, ionization) of the circumstellar medium and red giant wind into which the imminent nova ejecta will expand?

evidence.quote: In this first paper on our results, we present our pre-eruption observations made in ALMA frequency Bands 1, 3, 4, 6, 7, and 8 in August to November 2024 and constrain the properties of the environment into which the imminent next nova will erupt.
In this context, we present here pre-outburst ALMA observations of T CrB, aimed at characterizing the pre-eruption state of the object and the medium into which the nova ejecta will expand.

We analyzed our ALMA 2024 T CrB data and for comparison VLA 2016/17 data by (cite: 2019ApJ...884....8L) in order to determine the properties (density, temperature and ionization) of the stellar wind in which the upcoming nova will take place.
This paper makes use of the following ALMA data: ADS/JAO.ALMA#2023.A.00038.T, ADS/JAO.ALMA#2023.A.00041.S.

analysis_steps.goal: Model stellar wind density profile, temperature, density scale, and mass-loss rate

method.value: Apply an analytical isotropic, isothermal, fully ionized free-free stellar wind model in the hybrid optical depth regime: solve Eq. 2 for the wind density exponent beta from alpha, set lower limits on turnover frequency nu_t from the highest observed frequencies, and use Eqs. 3 and 6 to constrain the allowed (n0, T0) parameter space and mass-loss rate for candidate donor radii R.

evidence.quote: In order to interpret the VLA and ALMA spectra, we work with the simplified model inherited from (cite: 1975A&A....39....1P) and (cite: 1975MNRAS.170...41W): an isotropic, isothermal, fully ionized, and free-free emitting stellar wind.

To derive the uncertainty estimates given in [\[eq:beta1\]](#eq:beta1) and [\[eq:beta2\]](#eq:beta2), we solved equation [\[eq:p_indx\]](#eq:p_indx) for $\beta$ and then propagated the uncertainty values of spectral index $\alpha$ from Tables [3](#tab:specfit) and [4](#tab:vlaspectra) respectively into an uncertainty of the corresponding $\beta$.

We plot the relation $T_0(n_0)$ from $K$ for the two extreme potential values of $R$ and for 70 $R_\odot$, and we retain only the values which match the constraint from the corresponding turnover frequency’s lower limit.
The exact choice of $\nu_0$ has only a minor impact on the results, and so we set it to $30$ GHz, essentially the geometric mean of the VLA-ALMA frequency range.

Hereafter, we set a lower limit to the turnover frequency to the last data point of each dataset: $$\begin{align} &\nu_{\text{t,min},\text{2016/17}}=35~\text{GHz}\\ &\nu_{\text{t,min},\text{2024}}=350~\text{GHz} \end{align}$$
We plot the relation $T_0(n_0)$ from $K$ for the two extreme potential values of $R$ and for 70 $R_\odot$

assumptions.value: Isotropic, isothermal (T0 > 10^4 K), fully ionized wind with power-law density n(r) = n0 (r/R)^(-beta); Rayleigh-Jeans approximation (h*nu << k_B*T0); distance D ~ 895 pc; wind launch velocity = 10 km/s

evidence.quote: In the frequency range we span (5 GHz to 400 GHz) and for realistic wind temperatures ($T_0>10^4$ K such that the fully ionized hypothesis holds), we can make the Rayleigh-Jeans approximation ($h\nu\ll k_BT_0$)
Now, we use equation [\[eq:K\]](#eq:K) to obtain a relation between $n_0$, $R$ and $T_0$, knowing $\beta$ and using the distance $D\sim$895 pc (cite: 2021AJ....161..147B).

claims.experiment: Obtain concurrent ALMA observations in Bands 1, 3, 4, 6, and 7 at orbital phase 0.43 (plus supplemental Bands 1, 7, 8), fit a power-law SED, and compare with power-law fits to 13.5-35 GHz VLA spectra from 2016/17.
claims.result: In 2024, T CrB follows a power law with alpha = 0.56 +/- 0.11 and is ~5 times fainter extrapolated to 35 GHz than in 2016/17, where the average 13.5-35 GHz VLA spectral index was 0.90 +/- 0.02 (a difference of 0.34 +/- 0.11, or 0.26 +/- 0.13 relative to the softest VLA epoch).
claims.finding: T CrB in its 2024 pre-eruption quiescent state was significantly fainter and very likely had a softer spectrum around 40 GHz than during the 2016/17 high state.

evidence.quote: In the second half of 2024, after the end of its latest high state, the quiescent T CrB was a faint mm source with a spectral energy distribution well described by a powerlaw with index $\alpha=$0.56$\pm$0.11 and a flux density of ca. 0.1 mJy at 44 GHz and 0.4 mJy at 400 GHz.

evidence.loc: Spectral re-analysis of the 2016/17 VLA data
evidence.quote: Comparing the different spectral indices obtained from the VLA data from 2016/17 in the spectral range just below ours with the spectral index obtained from our observations in 2024, we can say that T CrB very likely had a softer spectrum around 40 GHz in 2024 than it had at any time during the VLA observations.

evidence.loc: Spectral re-analysis of the 2016/17 VLA data

claims.hypothesis: Both the 2016/17 VLA high-state spectrum and the 2024 ALMA quiescent spectrum can be explained by an isotropic, isothermal, fully-ionized free-free emitting red giant wind.
claims.experiment: Apply the analytical Panagia & Felli (1975) / Wright & Barlow (1975) ionized wind model in the hybrid optical depth regime to derive the wind density exponent beta and constrain (n0, T0) from the spectral normalization K and turnover frequency lower limits.
claims.result: For 2016/17, beta = 2.5 +/- 0.09 and the model yields allowed (n0, T0) solutions with mass-loss rate 1-5 x 10^-8 M_sun/yr; for 2024, beta = 2.0 +/- 0.11, but the low flux and high turnover frequency (>350 GHz) place all (n0, T0) curves inside the excluded region for any realistic donor radius R.
claims.finding: The fully-ionized isotropic wind model describes the 2016/17 high state well, but fails for the 2024 quiescent state, indicating that in 2024 the ionizing flux from the accretion disk was much lower and only a small fraction of the wind was ionized.

evidence.quote: A simple model of a free-free emitting, fully-ionized stellar wind seems to describe well the 2016/17 high state of T CrB but not our 2024 ALMA measurements with their low flux and high turnover frequency suggesting that in 2024, the wind was far from fully ionized.

The stellar mass loss rate we measure is in the range 1 to 5$\times 10^{-8}$M$_{\odot}/$yr, in agreement with the expected values from the accretion rate during the high-state (cite: 2004A&A...415..609S) and from the recurrence period of the nova (cite: 2023JHA....54..436S).

However, the 2024 ALMA data cannot be interpreted with this model. Indeed, the flux is too low and the turnover frequency too high to yield a range of possible values for $n_0$ and $T_0$, for any realistic stellar radius $R$.
